title: EvoPresent: Self-Improving Presentation Agents
one_liner: A self-improvement agent learns to score and adjust presentation aesthetics, so presentations can iterate toward better visual and narrative quality.
lead: Academic papers live or die by how well they are presented. But making a great presentation by hand takes skill: the slides need to look good, tell a coherent story, and keep viewers interested. This paper introduces EvoPresent, an agent that watches presentations, grades their aesthetics, spots problems (like cluttered slides or weak narration), and suggests fixes. Then it tries again. The agent improves through repeated self-correction because each score tells it whether the last change moved in the right direction, so it learns which edits work.

paras: Today, when you use software to create a slide deck or video presentation automatically, the output is predictable: text crammed into corners, images placed randomly, and narration that recites facts without drama. The software made something, but nobody wants to watch it.

A beginner might try to improve this by adding more rules: Make text bigger. Use brighter colors. But rules are rigid. One rule breaks another. And most importantly, you have no way to judge whether your fix actually made things better, because aesthetic quality is vague and context-dependent. There is no objective score, so the system has nowhere to aim.

callout.html: An automated presentation system cannot improve itself without a reliable way to measure whether it succeeded, because without measurement, any change is equally likely to make things worse, so there is no signal to learn from.

panels.title: 1. The problem
panels.caption: Automated presentations are dull: text everywhere, colors clash, no clear story.

panels.title: 2. The evaluation bottleneck
panels.caption: Without a score, you cannot tell if a change is better or worse.

panels.title: 3. The paper introduces PresAesth
panels.caption: A neural model that scores aesthetics. Bright areas mean worse, dim means better.

panels.title: 4. The agent acts on the feedback
panels.caption: Agent gets a score and makes tweaks: remove clutter, improve layout, strengthen narration.

panels.title: 5. Iterate: score again, adjust again
panels.caption: After each fix, the aesthetic score climbs. Better presentations in rounds.

steps.text: A trained neural model scores a slide presentation on aesthetics: layout clarity, color harmony, visual balance, text readability.
The model flags specific problems: overcrowded text, misaligned elements, weak color contrast.
The agent sees the score and the defect list, and knows: this presentation scored 3 out of 10 aesthetically.

The agent modifies the presentation (reorganizes slides, simplifies text, improves visual hierarchy, rewrites narration) because the feedback identified specific defects, so targeted changes have a chance to work.
Re-evaluate. Score is now 5 out of 10. Adjust again. After many rounds, score reaches 8.

paras: The agent modifies the presentation itself: slide layouts, text content and size, color choices, image placement, and the script that a virtual character reads aloud. Each iteration changes these elements based on feedback from the aesthetic scorer.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: presentation aesthetic score
hidden.name: Aesthetic coherence and visual quality
paras: Aesthetics in presentations is normally invisible and unmeasurable. This paper gives it a concrete name and measure: the aesthetic score. It captures how visually balanced a slide is, how readable the text, how well colors harmonize, and how clear the visual hierarchy — whether the slide guides the viewer's eye to what matters.

PresAesth (the neural model) estimates this score from a presentation's visual features. It also performs two related tasks: identifying specific defects (cluttered layout, weak contrast, unclear narration) and comparing two presentations to say which one is more aesthetically pleasing. All three tasks train together.

heat.caption: Darker shade means stronger aesthetic strength. Highlighted cells are the defects the model flagged.

reads.html: The aesthetic score is a number from 0 to 10 that summarizes how good a presentation looks and feels to a viewer: clear, engaging, balanced, readable.

PresAesth is a multi-task RL aesthetic model that jointly learns to score presentations, identify visual defects, and rank pairs by aesthetic quality. It provides numerical feedback to the self-improvement agent.

mechanism.h2: Why self-correction via scoring actually works
paras: The core insight: an agent cannot improve something it cannot measure, because without a measurement, it has no way to know whether a change moved toward the goal or away from it. If you say 'make the presentation better' but offer no score, the agent has no signal to learn from and will thrash randomly, because every change is equally likely to succeed or fail.

By giving the agent a reliable aesthetic score (from PresAesth), the agent gains a clear goal. Every change can be judged: Did the score go up? If yes, keep that kind of change. If no, try something different. Over many rounds, the agent learns which tweaks move the score in the right direction, because the feedback is immediate and unambiguous. It builds intuition about what makes presentations work.

The score must be high-quality and reliable. The paper shows that if the scorer is noisy or biased, the agent learns bad habits and stalls, because it is optimizing for the wrong target. But with a well-trained scorer, the agent reliably improves itself, even starting from poor presentations. The multi-task training (scoring + defect detection + comparison) makes PresAesth effective because it learns from multiple angles at once. Different viewpoints catch errors that a single viewpoint would miss.

stages.s: PresAesth scores aesthetics and flags defects
Agent receives score (e.g., 4/10) and defect list
Agent modifies (reorganizes layout, simplifies text, improves colors) because the defects show exactly what to fix
Revised presentation, ready to score again

math.words: The agent uses PresAesth's score as a reward signal in reinforcement learning. Formally, the agent learns a policy (a strategy for editing slides) that maximizes expected aesthetic score, where the score comes from multiple evaluation tasks.
symbols: Direct rating of a single presentation on a 0-10 scale
How well the model identifies specific visual problems
How well the model ranks two presentations by quality
Combine the three scores, giving each one appropriate importance

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Presentation A: aesthetics rating 4/10, defect detection accuracy 0.7, ranking task accuracy 0.6.
Agent adjusts: removes clutter (improves aesthetics to 6), improves layout consistency (defect accuracy rises to 0.85), clearer visual hierarchy (ranking accuracy rises to 0.8).
Agent sees the improvement and learns: this kind of change (simplify, align, emphasize) boosts the score.

math.note: The multi-task score ensures the agent learns balanced improvement: not just high ratings, but actually fixing real defects and winning comparisons against alternatives.

bars.h2: Before and after: self-improvement in action

charts.title: Naive automated system (no feedback loop)
charts.note: Without reliable feedback, the system makes random changes. Progress stalls because it cannot tell whether adjustments help.

charts.title: EvoPresent (with PresAesth scoring)
charts.note: With a reliable score, the agent makes targeted improvements. Each round the score climbs, showing real progress. By round 3, the presentation is engaging and well-designed.

items.html: If PresAesth itself is poorly trained, it gives bad feedback. The agent then learns to game the bad scorer, making presentations that score high but look worse to humans, because the agent optimizes for whatever signal it receives. The paper shows this explicitly: a bad scorer leads to no real improvement because the agent chases the wrong target.

items.b: Agent gets stuck optimizing one narrow metric.
items.html: If the score only measures text size, the agent will make all text huge and wreck the layout. The multi-task training helps: scoring + defect + comparison together prevent narrow optimization, because balancing three different viewpoints prevents the agent from chasing a single proxy that diverges from real quality. But if the weights are wrong, one task can dominate and unbalance improvement.

The agent adjusts slides and narration separately. If they lose sync (e.g., the voice describes a diagram that no longer appears), the presentation becomes confusing. The model must jointly optimize all modalities.

When PresAesth is trained on diverse presentations with real human feedback, and the agent is given all three tasks (score, defect, rank) with balanced weights, presentations reliably improve across many rounds, because the aligned feedback signal and balanced objectives eliminate both noise and narrow gaming.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Take a real academic paper. Generate an initial presentation automatically (minimal effort). Let EvoPresent iterate for 5 rounds. Measure the aesthetic score at each step. Also ask humans: does this presentation tell the story clearly? Is it engaging? Does it guide your eye to the key claims?
demo.metric_eq: Improvement = aesthetic_score_round_5 - aesthetic_score_round_1; Human preference rate = fraction of judges who prefer round 5 over round 1
demo.closing: The demo must show that the aesthetic score climbs monotonically (or mostly monotonically) with each iteration, proving the feedback loop works and the agent is learning from its scores. It must also show human judges agree the later presentations are genuinely better to watch, because correlation between algorithm and human judgment validates that PresAesth is capturing real quality.
